2.caption: Figure 2 : The overview of HIFOR. (a) We augment the VLA with hierarchical foresight prediction and action-guided world retrieval, enabling the Action Expert to leverage future information during action generation. (b) Hierarchical Foresight Prediction (§ 3.4 ) predicts short-term, milestone, and goal futures through hierarchical dependency modeling. (c) Structure-Aware Latent World Modeling (§ 3.5 ) organizes future latent representations along the horizon, view, and spatial dimensions. (d) Action-Guided Factorized World Retrieval (§ 3.6 ) selectively retrieves action-relevant future information through denoising-aware factorized attention to guide action generation.

1.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of AR-WAM. An agent grounds the target and issues a visual prompt g g together with an atomic operation s s . A compact 0.5B world action model (a 0.2B transformer shared by a reasoning expert and a world action expert, plus a frozen 0.3B vision encoder) predicts an action chunk together with dual-level foresight signals. The reasoning expert runs once per control cycle, and the world action expert then performs multi-step denoising while reusing its KV cache.

1.caption: Fig. 1: WorldContact overview. (Left): an agent-verified physical-simulation dataset, where an automated simulation agent samples the object and prescribed state and executes the resulting controls in the physical simulator. (Middle): contact-centric world model prediction and rendering of object-state trajectories into the observation modality consumed by the VLA. (Right): VLA fine-tuning for task-specific policy adaptation and subsequent real-robot deployment.

2.caption: Fig. 2: WorldContact pipeline. Given the current object state and prescribed state, WorldContact proceeds through four stages: the contact-centric vertex tokenizer encodes spatial, topological, controllable, and environmental contact information into vertex tokens; the hierarchical encoder merges vertex tokens into global tokens for long-range communication; and the global-token decoder refines vertex tokens to produce vertex-level state corrections. A differentiable projection is used to improve long-horizon rollout stability during fine-tuning.

1.caption: Fig. 1: Evolution of World-Action Models. The timeline summarizes representative milestones from latent world-model reinforcement learning and foundation vision-language-action models to video-action models, and recent unified World-Action Models. It highlights how predictive modeling and action generation have gradually converged toward integrated frameworks for embodied robot control.

2.caption:
Fig. 2: Conceptual overview of four foundational threads behind WAMs: (a) world models learn latent dynamics by predicting the next state from current state and action; (b) video generative models predict future visual observations conditioned on visual history and language instruction; (c) latent action pretraining infers latent actions from consecutive frames and uses them to model latent transitions; and (d) VLAs generate future action sequences directly from state and language instructions.
(The third-row illustrations are adapted from the corresponding papers cited in each thread.)

1.caption: Figure 1 : Conceptual comparison of existing WAMs and SG-WAM. Whereas explicit and auxiliary latent targets may introduce perceptual burden or target–policy mismatch, SG-WAM learns intervening-action-conditioned dynamics in geometry-structured, policy-derived representations.

2.caption: Figure 2 : Overview of the SG-WAM framework. The VLM jointly contextualizes multi-view observations, language, and learnable dynamics tokens for action generation. During training, a frozen VGGT teacher shapes main-view image tokens, while SGWP predicts future dynamics-token states conditioned on intervening actions and aligns them with an EMA policy target. All auxiliary branches are removed at inference.

2.caption:
Figure 2 : Temporal evolution of representative works on world models for robotic policy learning.
The upper branch summarizes the progression of world model for policy methods , showing a trend from early decoupled video-generation-plus-IDM pipelines toward tighter integration through single-backbone, MoE/MoT, unified VLA, and latent world-modeling designs.
The lower branch summarizes the progression of world model as simulator methods , where world models evolve from rollout-based validation and candidate evaluation into learned simulators for policy reinforcement learning, post-training, and co-evolving optimization.
These trends should be understood as dominant directions rather than strictly sequential replacements.

2.caption: Figure 2 : GR00T N1 Model Overview. Our model is a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model that adopts a dual-system design. We convert the image observation and language instruction into a sequence of tokens to be processed by the Vision-Language Model (VLM) backbone. 3.caption: Fig. 3: Overview of our framework. We start with a pre-training mixture, which consists of both our own dexterous manipulation datasets and open-source data. We use this mixture to train our flow matching VLA model, which consists of a larger VLM backbone and a smaller action expert for processing robot states and actions. The VLM backbone weights are initialized from PaliGemma [ 5 ] , providing representations learned from large-scale Internet pre-training. The resulting π 0 \pi_{0} model can be used to control multiple robot embodiments with differing action spaces to accomplish a wide variety of tasks.

1.caption: Fig. 1: Pose-robust actuation co-design for tendon-driven robot hands (PACT) framework. The framework combines a force-pose library, task-specific bandwidth constraints, and actuator properties to jointly optimize tendon-driven robot hands. It shapes feasible force sets across representative poses, maximizes the workspace coverage under worst-joint bandwidth limits, and selects design parameters that balance force capability, motion speed, and pose robustness. The resulting parameters define the tendon-routing and actuation configuration of the optimized hand.

1.caption: Figure 1: Overview of non-episodic training in CRONOS. We introduce CRONOS, a benchmark for RL fine-tuning of VLAs under infrequent scene resets. Tasks share a scene (top left). Episodic training resets the scene before every task, whereas non-episodic training continues each task from where the previous one ended. CRONOS covers diverse scenes and objects (middle left). Without frequent resets, object positions become increasingly dispersed, and rollout success decays after each scene reset (bottom). Yet policies fine-tuned non-episodically generalize better to unseen object positions and perform better on unseen task sequences (right).

2.caption:
Figure 2: Architecture of HiLo-WAM. HiLo-WAM builds on a dual-DiT World Action Model consisting of a shared
Video DiT and an Action DiT.
The visual world is modeled at two complementary temporal scales:
a sparse long-horizon visual stream captures historical context and coarse
future evolution, while a dense local visual dynamics stream captures
fine-grained local interactions.
Both visual streams are jointly modeled with robot actions.
During inference, the visual streams progressively terminate and are cached,
while the action stream continues denoising to completion.

1.caption: Figure 1: Evolution of human-to-robot learning paradigms. (a) MoCap-based methods depend on specialized capture devices, so data remains costly to collect, and the large embodiment gap limits generalization. (b) Latent action learning is trained directly from abundant raw human videos, but the learned representations are contaminated by scene noise. (c) Our method also learns from easy-to-acquire raw videos, yet extracts a clean Action Intent shared across humans and robots, enabling noise-free knowledge transfer to the robot.

1.caption:
Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed training framework. Given multi-view images, we first estimate the physical properties of the manipulated object by combining feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF-3DGS) with MPM via a differentiable physical simulation.
The simulator is coupled with a differentiable rasterizer and optimized under video guidance, where gradients are back-propagated through the simulation. Physics-based constraints, including Dirichlet boundary conditions for manipulation events and geometric consistency via temporal Chamfer distance, further regularize the estimated physical parameters by aligning simulated particle dynamics with demonstration videos.
The learned physical parameters are then injected into a physical-aware diffusion policy as physics conditions, together with language instructions and visual observations,
